passages.t: The one You love is sick
passages.happening:
A man named Lazarus is sick. He lives in Bethany with his sisters, Mary and Martha (verse 1). John tells us this Mary is the one who will later pour perfume on Jesus' feet and wipe them with her hair (verse 2).

The sisters send Jesus a short message: “Lord, the one You love is sick” (verse 3). When Jesus hears it, he says, “This sickness will not end in death. No, it is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (verse 4).

Then John puts two sentences side by side. “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.” And: “So on hearing that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was for two days” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem, ‘a little less than two miles away’ (verse 18). Jesus was across the Jordan, where chapter 10 left him, some distance away. The Arab town on the site today is called al-Eizariya, a name that comes from Lazarus, and Christians have pointed to a tomb there as his since at least the fourth century.

The name Lazarus is a Greek form of the Hebrew name Eleazar, which means ‘God has helped’. Martha and Mary are known from Luke's Gospel too, where Martha is busy serving and Mary sits at Jesus' feet (Luke 10:38-42).

Notice what the sisters' message does not say. They do not ask Jesus to come. They do not tell him what to do. They simply tell him who is sick: the one you love. They trust that love will be enough to bring him.

‘Will not end in death’ does not mean Lazarus will not die. He does. It means death will not have the last word in this story.
passages.ot: The Scriptures already told of God giving back the dead. When Elijah prayed for a widow's son, “the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah, and the child’s life returned to him, and he lived” (1 Kings 17:22). And the prophets looked further, to a final day: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19).
passages.hard:
Why did Jesus wait two days, if he loved them? John does not hide the question. He puts the love and the delay in the same breath, and later both sisters will say, ‘Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died’ (verses 21 and 32). Bystanders ask it too (verse 37).

Christians have answered in several ways. Some stress Jesus' purpose: he meant to do something greater than a healing, so that people would see God's glory and believe (verses 4 and 15). Some readers count the days: a day for the message to reach him, two days' wait, and a day's travel come to the four days of verse 17, so Lazarus may already have died before the messenger arrived. Others note that in John, Jesus acts at his Father's time, not at anyone else's (2:4, 7:6).

None of these answers takes the pain away, and the chapter does not pretend it does. What it shows is that the delay was not lack of love. John says so plainly in verse 5, and the rest of the chapter shows Jesus weeping at the grave.
passages.asks: Many people have prayed ‘Lord, the one You love is sick’ and then waited, and the answer did not come as they hoped. This passage does not explain every delay, and it does not promise that every sick person will get well. It does say that being loved by Jesus and facing a long, frightening wait can both be true at once. The sisters' prayer is a good one to borrow. It tells him who is hurting, and it trusts his love.

passages.t: Let us go, so that we may die with Him
passages.happening:
After the two days Jesus says, “Let us go back to Judea” (verse 7). The disciples are alarmed. “Rabbi,” they reply, “the Jews just tried to stone You, and You are going back there?” (verse 8).

Jesus answers with a picture. “Are there not twelve hours of daylight? If anyone walks in the daytime, he will not stumble” (verse 9). Then he says, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to wake him up” (verse 11). The disciples take him literally: “Lord, if he is sleeping, he will get better” (verse 12). So Jesus tells them plainly, “Lazarus is dead,” and, “for your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him” (verses 14-15).

Thomas speaks for them all: “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
‘The Jews’ in verse 8 means the leaders and crowd in Jerusalem who had picked up stones in chapter 10 (10:31). Judea was dangerous for Jesus now, and the disciples knew it.

‘Twelve hours of daylight’ was a common way to count a day. Jesus means that his time is set by the Father. As long as his ‘day’ lasts, no one can cut it short. He can walk into danger without stumbling.

Calling death ‘sleep’ was an old and gentle way of speaking, used in the Scriptures for those who have died. Jesus uses it with a new meaning. For him, waking Lazarus will be as easy as waking a sleeper.

Thomas is often remembered as ‘doubting Thomas’, from a later chapter. Here he is the brave one. He expects Jesus to be killed in Judea, and he decides to go and die with him. His courage is real, even if his understanding is not yet complete.
passages.ot: Daniel spoke of the dead as sleepers: “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2). Paul later used the same picture for believers who had died, writing so that Christians “will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
passages.asks: Thomas did not understand everything, but he was willing to go where Jesus was going. Faith sometimes looks like that: not certainty about the outcome, but loyalty to the person. If you feel more like Thomas than like a hero, notice that his loyalty was enough to keep him walking with Jesus.

passages.t: I am the resurrection and the life
passages.happening:
When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days (verse 17). Many people from Jerusalem have come to comfort Martha and Mary (verses 18-19). When Martha hears that Jesus is coming, she goes out to meet him. Mary stays at home (verse 20).

Martha says, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that God will give You whatever You ask of Him” (verses 21-22). Jesus tells her, “Your brother will rise again” (verse 23). She answers, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day” (verse 24).

Jesus says, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies. And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?” (verses 25-26). “Yes, Lord,” Martha answers, “I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Four days mattered. Later rabbinic writings, written down centuries after Jesus, record a belief that for three days after death the soul stays near the body, and then leaves. Whether people in Jesus' day believed that is not certain. Either way, four days meant there was no doubt left. Lazarus was dead.

Mourning was shared. Friends and neighbors came to the house to sit with the family. That is why so many people from Jerusalem are there.

Martha's hope was the hope of many Jews in her day: that God would raise the dead on the last day. The Pharisees taught it. The Sadducees, the party of many chief priests, denied it. Jesus does not correct her. He takes her hope and puts it in himself. The resurrection is not only an event at the end of time. It is a person, and he is standing in front of her.

Martha's confession is one of the greatest in the Gospels. It matches the reason John says he wrote the whole book: so that readers ‘may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God’ (20:31). In the other Gospels Peter makes a confession like it. In John, it is Martha, in the middle of her grief.
passages.ot: Daniel's promise stood behind Martha's hope: “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Daniel 12:2). Isaiah promised that God “will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face” (Isaiah 25:8). Job held on to the same hope in his suffering: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth” (Job 19:25).
passages.hard:
‘Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies’ and ‘everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die’ can sound like a contradiction. Believers do die. Lazarus himself, after being raised, would die again. Jesus is speaking of two kinds of death. The body's death still comes. But the life Jesus gives is not ended by it. Those who belong to him die, and still live, and will rise.

Christians confess this in the Apostles' Creed: ‘the resurrection of the body, and the life everlasting’. The chapter does not promise that anyone's loved one will be brought back now, as Lazarus was. Lazarus came back to this life, and in time he would die again. What Jesus promises is more than that, and it waits for the last day.
passages.asks: Martha came to Jesus with grief and a complaint, ‘If You had been here’, and also with faith. Jesus did not scold her for the complaint. He answered her and drew out her faith. You can bring both to him too. Grief is not unbelief, and an honest ‘why’ is not a lack of faith.

passages.happening:
Martha goes back and tells Mary quietly, “The Teacher is here and is asking for you” (verse 28). Mary gets up quickly and goes to him. The mourners in the house follow her, thinking she is going to the tomb to weep (verses 29-31).

When Mary reaches Jesus, she falls at his feet and says what Martha said: “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died” (verse 32). When Jesus sees her weeping, and the people with her weeping too, “He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled” (verse 33). “Where have you put him?” he asks. “Come and see, Lord,” they answer (verse 34).

“Jesus wept” (verse 35).

Some of the people say, “See how He loved him!” (verse 36). Others ask, “Could not this man who opened the eyes of the blind also have kept Lazarus from dying?” (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
‘Deeply moved’ is a strong Greek word, embrimaomai. It is used elsewhere for a stern warning (Mark 1:43) and for people scolding someone (Mark 14:5). It carries a sense of strong feeling, and often of anger or indignation. Some Bibles note that it could be rendered ‘deeply indignant’. Readers differ on what Jesus was angry at. Many think it was death itself, the enemy that tears families apart. Some think it was the unbelief around him. Others think the word here holds anger and grief together. What is clear is that Jesus was not calm or distant at the grave.

‘Jesus wept’ is two words in English. John uses a different verb for Jesus' tears than for the mourners' loud weeping in verse 33. The word for Jesus usually means simply to shed tears. The crowd's grief was loud, as mourning often was. Jesus' tears may have been quieter.

Why weep, if he knew he was about to raise Lazarus? Because the grief in front of him was real. Mary was broken, his friends were weeping, and death is a real enemy. Jesus did not stand above their sorrow. He entered it.

The bystanders' two reactions show the two ways people still look at Jesus' tears. Some see love. Others see a question: if he could have stopped it, why didn't he?
passages.ot: The Psalms say God keeps account of tears: “Put my tears in Your bottle” (Psalm 56:8). Isaiah described the coming servant as “a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3). The wise man wrote that there is “a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance” (Ecclesiastes 3:4). Joseph mourned for his father seven days (Genesis 50:10).
passages.asks:
If you are grieving, hear this clearly: grief is not unbelief. Jesus knew that resurrection was coming, and he still wept. Your tears do not mean your faith has failed. They mean you loved someone, and that death is as wrong as Jesus showed it to be.

If you have lost someone and no miracle came, this story does not say you were loved less than Martha and Mary. Lazarus was given back for a while, and in time he would die again. The promise Jesus made to Martha, the resurrection at the last day, is the same promise he makes to everyone who trusts him. The one who wept at Lazarus' grave does not stand at a distance from yours. If grief is crushing you, do not carry it alone. Reach out to people you trust, to a pastor, or to someone trained to help.

passages.happening:
Jesus, deeply moved again, comes to the tomb. It is a cave with a stone across the entrance (verse 38). “Take away the stone,” he says. Martha objects: “Lord, by now he stinks,” and, “It has already been four days” (verse 39). Jesus answers, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” (verse 40).

They take away the stone. Jesus looks up and prays: “Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. I knew that You always hear Me, but I say this for the benefit of the people standing here, so they may believe that You sent Me” (verses 41-42).

Then he calls out in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” (verse 43). The man who had been dead comes out, his hands and feet bound with strips of linen and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus tells them, “Unwrap him and let him go” (verse 44).
passages.hearers:
Around Jerusalem, families buried their dead in tombs cut into the soft rock, often caves with a low entrance closed by a stone. The body was wrapped in strips of cloth, with a separate cloth over the face. John will describe the same kind of cloths later, left lying in Jesus' own empty tomb (20:5-7).

Martha's objection is honest and practical. She has faith in Jesus, but she cannot imagine what he is about to do. Few people could have.

Jesus' prayer is unusual. He thanks the Father before anything happens, as if the answer were already given. He says the prayer out loud for the sake of the people watching, so that they will know where his power comes from. He does not act on his own. He acts as the one the Father sent.

‘Unwrap him and let him go’ gives the people around Lazarus a part to play. Jesus gives life. Then he tells the community to help free the man from what still binds him.
passages.ot: Ezekiel heard God promise his people, “I will open your graves and bring you up from them” (Ezekiel 37:12). Hosea asked, “Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?” (Hosea 13:14). The prophets' hope of a final victory over death is pictured here in one man coming out of one tomb.
passages.hard: Did this really happen? Matthew, Mark and Luke do not mention Lazarus, and some scholars think the story grew up later. Others answer that those three Gospels tell much less of Jesus' time near Jerusalem, that they do tell of other people raised from the dead (Mark 5:21-43; Luke 7:11-17), and that John says the chief priests planned to kill Lazarus too (12:10), which may be why the earlier Gospels left his name out. These notes do not try to settle what historians can prove. John tells it as a sign: a real event that points beyond itself to the one who is the resurrection and the life.
passages.asks: Lazarus came out still bound, and others had to help unwrap him. New life often begins like that. If Jesus has called you out of something that felt like a tomb, you may still need others to help you get free of what clings to you. And if someone near you is just stepping out, you may be one of the people Jesus is asking to help unwrap them.

passages.happening:
Many of the people who had come to Mary see what Jesus did and believe in him. But some go to the Pharisees and report it (verses 45-46).

The chief priests and Pharisees call a meeting of the Sanhedrin, the high council. “What are we to do? This man is performing many signs. If we let Him go on like this, everyone will believe in Him, and then the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (verses 47-48).

Caiaphas, the high priest that year, answers, “You know nothing at all! You do not realize that it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish” (verses 49-50). John explains that Caiaphas did not say this on his own. As high priest he was prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation, “and not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one” (verse 52). From that day on they plotted to kill him (verse 53).
passages.hearers:
Notice who is in this scene. Many Jews who saw the sign believed in Jesus (verse 45). The plot is not the act of a people. It is the decision of a particular council, led by particular men, in one meeting. John's book page explains why that matters.

The Sanhedrin was the Jewish high council in Jerusalem, made up of chief priests, elders and teachers of the Law, and led by the high priest. Under Roman rule it had power only as long as Rome allowed it. The leaders' fear was real. Rome crushed popular movements that gathered around a would-be king. ‘Our place’ probably means the temple, and ‘our nation’ their people's limited freedom.

Caiaphas was high priest for many years, from about AD 18 until about AD 36 or 37, appointed and later removed by the Romans. John calls him high priest ‘that year’, the year that mattered most. His reasoning was cold: better that one man die than that the council lose everything. John hears in his words a meaning he never intended. Jesus would indeed die for the people, not to keep Rome away, but to gather God's scattered children into one.

The irony is sharp. The leaders feared that the Romans would come and take the place and the nation. In AD 70, about forty years later, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. Killing Jesus did not prevent what they feared.
passages.ot: The high priest once carried the Urim and Thummim, used to seek God's will, “over Aaron’s heart whenever he comes before the LORD” (Exodus 28:30). John sees God speaking through Caiaphas' office even when the man himself meant something else. The ‘one shepherd’ who gathers the flock echoes Ezekiel 34:23, and Jesus' own words in 10:16.
passages.hard:
Is John blaming the Jewish people for Jesus' death? No. This verse, like others in the passion story, has been misused to blame Jews as a people, and that misuse is false. John names a council and its leaders, and he says that many other Jews believed (verse 45). Later the order to crucify will come from a Roman governor, and Roman soldiers will carry it out. The New Testament places all people inside the guilt: in Acts the first Christians pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel all stood together against Jesus (Acts 4:27).

Caiaphas' line, ‘better that one man die’, is also a warning for every age. Leaders of every kind, religious or not, have reasoned that way, sacrificing one person to protect an institution. The cross shows where that reasoning leads, and God used even that to save.
passages.asks: Caiaphas said ‘one man for the people’ to protect his own position. God turned his words into the gospel: one man for the people, so that the scattered could be gathered. If you have been sacrificed by someone else's calculation, Jesus has stood where you stand. And his death was for people like you, to gather you in.

passages.t: Will He come to the feast?
passages.happening:
Because of the plot, Jesus no longer moves about openly. He withdraws to a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness, and stays there with his disciples (verse 54).

Passover is near. Many people go up to Jerusalem early to purify themselves before the feast (verse 55). In the temple courts they keep looking for Jesus and asking one another, “What do you think? Will He come to the feast at all?” (verse 56). The chief priests and Pharisees have given orders that anyone who knows where he is must report it, so that they can arrest him (verse 57).
passages.hearers:
Where Ephraim was is not certain. It was a small town near the wilderness, probably north of Jerusalem. It gave Jesus a quiet place for a short time before the end.

Purifying before Passover was part of the Law. Anyone who had become unclean, for example by touching a dead body, could not eat the Passover until they were made clean again. So people came up days early. The city filled with pilgrims, and the talk was all about Jesus.

This is the third Passover John mentions (2:13, 6:4), and the last. The questions at the temple set the stage for chapter 12, when Jesus comes to Bethany and then rides into Jerusalem.
passages.ot: The Law said, “Whoever touches any dead body will be unclean for seven days” (Numbers 19:11), and in Moses' day “there were some men who were unclean due to a dead body, so they could not observe the Passover on that day” (Numbers 9:6). Passover itself remembered the night God freed Israel from Egypt, and the lamb whose blood marked the doors.
passages.asks: ‘Will He come to the feast at all?’ The crowd asked it as gossip. The Gospel answers it with the cross. Jesus did come, knowing what waited for him. The one who wept at Lazarus' grave went on toward his own, for the sake of the people he loved.
